results.title: Create a Safety & Security Framework
results.requirement: Define a state-of-the-art Safety and Security Framework that conceptually describes how systemic risks are assessed, accepted, and mitigated across the model lifecycle.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define, at a conceptual and descriptive level, the key elements required for systemic risk management under the Safety and Security Chapter (including trigger points, risk acceptance logic, mitigation expectations, responsibility allocation, external input, and update processes)?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly describes its purpose as managing systemic risks associated with general-purpose AI models.
The framework outlines how systemic risks are identified, assessed, and mitigated at a high level.
The framework describes trigger points at which additional evaluations or assessments would occur during the model lifecycle.
The framework defines how systemic risk acceptability is determined, including the use of risk tiers or acceptance criteria.
The framework describes, at a high level, expected categories or types of safety and security mitigations associated with different risk levels.
The framework explains how responsibility for systemic risk assessment and mitigation is allocated within the organization.
The framework describes whether and how input from external actors may influence risk-related decisions.
The framework describes how and under what conditions the framework itself would be reviewed or updated.

Indicative concepts and phrases: framework scope, systemic risk management, trigger points, risk acceptance criteria, mitigation expectations, responsibility allocation, external input, framework update process
results.reasoning: The text covers trigger points, risk acceptance criteria with tiers, mitigations, responsibility allocation, external input, and framework update processes, addressing the core lifecycle elements. It lacks an explicit standalone purpose statement describing that the framework is intended to manage systemic risks across general-purpose AI models, and mitigation categorization is described only at a high level without enumerated concrete types. Alignment indicators claim an explicit purpose but the source text does not include it, indicating alignment overreach and a gap that prevents full compliance.
key_aligned_concepts: Trigger points and lighter-touch evaluations across the model lifecycle
Systemic risk acceptance criteria and risk tiers with associated mitigations
Allocation of responsibility for systemic risk assessment and mitigation
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Missing explicit purpose statement: the framework does not explicitly state that its purpose is to manage systemic risks associated with general-purpose AI models across the model lifecycle.
Mitigation categorization is high-level and not explicitly enumerated by tier with concrete categories/types mapped to each risk tier.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Yes; the framework describes trigger points, risk acceptance criteria with tiers, mitigations, responsibility allocation, external input, and framework update processes across the model lifecycle to manage systemic risks.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text provides high-level governance elements (trigger points, risk tiers, mitigations, responsibilities, external input, and update processes) that align with the EU requirement for a state-of-the-art Safety and Security Framework governing systemic risk across the model lifecycle.
key_aligned_concepts: Trigger points and lighter-touch evaluations across the model lifecycle
Systemic risk acceptance criteria and risk tiers with associated mitigations
Allocation of responsibility for systemic risk assessment and mitigation

A Framework assessment will include the following: 
(1) Framework adequacy: An assessment of whether the processes and measures in the 
Framework are appropriate for the systemic risks stemming from the Signatories’ models. 
This assessment will take into account how the models are currently being developed,  
made available on the market, and/or used, and how they are expected to be developed, 
made available on the market, and/or used over the next 12 months. 
(2) Framework adherence: An assessment focused on the Signatories’ adherence to the 
Framework, including: (a) any instances of, and reasons for, non-adherence to the Framework 
since the last Framework assessment; and (b) any measures, including safety and security 
mitigations, that need to be implemented to ensure continued adherence to the Framework. 
If point(s) (a) and/or (b) give rise to risks of future non-adherence, Signatories will make 
remediation plans as part of their Framework assessment.

thereof, within five business days of either being confirmed.

Measure 1.2 Implementing the Framework 
Signatories will implement the processes and measures outlined in their Framework as specified in 
the following paragraphs. 
Along the entire model lifecycle, Signatories will continuously: 
(1) assess the systemic risks stemming from the model by: 
(a) conducting lighter-touch model evaluations that need not adhere to Appendix 3 (e.g. 
automated evaluations) at appropriate trigger points defined in terms of, e.g. time, 
training compute, development stages, user access, inference compute, and/or 
affordances;

(2) analysing each identified systemic risk as specified in Commitment 3; 
(3) determining whether the systemic risks stemming from the model are acceptable as specified 
in Measure 4.1; and 
(4) if the systemic risks stemming from the model are not determined to be acceptable, 
implementing safety and/or security mitigations as specified in Commitments 5 and 6, and 
re-assessing the systemic risks stemming from the model starting from point (1), as specified 
in Measure 4.2. 
Signatories will conduct such a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process at least before 
placing the model on the market and whenever the conditions specified in Measure 7.6, first and 
third paragraph, are met. Signatories will report their implemented measures and processes to the 
AI Office as specified in Commitment 7.

updated, along with a version number and the date of change.

results.title: Implement the Safety & Security Framework
results.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework is intended to be applied across the entire model lifecycle, including continuous systemic risk assessment activities, trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident inputs, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how its systemic risk assessment and mitigation processes are intended to be applied across the model lifecycle, including continuous assessment activities, trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident consideration, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment?
expected_evidence: The framework describes how systemic risks are continuously assessed along the entire model lifecycle.
The framework explains how lighter-touch evaluations are conducted at predefined trigger points (e.g. based on time, development stage, compute, access, or affordances).
The framework describes how post-market monitoring is conducted to inform ongoing systemic risk assessment.
The framework explains how information about serious incidents or near misses is taken into account within the risk assessment process.

The framework describes how results from trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, or incident inputs can lead to deeper analysis or escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process.
The framework outlines the sequence or structure of the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (identification, analysis, acceptability determination, mitigation, and re-assessment).

Indicative concepts and phrases: continuous implementation, lifecycle application, trigger-point evaluation, post-market monitoring, incident inputs, escalation, full systemic risk assessment, mitigation cycle
results.reasoning: Indicators 1–3 and 5–6 are evidenced (continuous lifecycle risk assessment, trigger-point lighter evaluations, post-market monitoring, escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process, and the defined four-step full risk assessment sequence). However, Indicator 4 (explicit incorporation and handling of near-miss incident inputs to inform systemic risk assessments) is not evidenced in the text. The analysis only references serious incidents; near-miss inputs are not clearly incorporated. Since this is a binary operational requirement, its absence cannot be offset by thematic alignment, leading to a NOT_COMPLIANT designation.
key_aligned_concepts: Escalation to full systemic risk assessment and mitigation
Full systemic risk assessment sequence (identification, analysis, acceptability determination, mitigation, and re-assessment)
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Missing explicit incorporation and handling of near-miss incident inputs to inform systemic risk assessments and trigger escalation.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Yes—the framework describes continuous systemic risk assessment across the entire model lifecycle, lighter-touch trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident inputs, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process with a four-step sequence (identification, analysis, acceptability determination, mitigation, and re-assessment).
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text covers continuous lifecycle risk assessment, trigger-based lighter evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident inputs, and escalation to a formal full systemic risk assessment with a defined process, meeting the core elements of the EU requirement.
key_aligned_concepts: Escalation to full systemic risk assessment and mitigation
Full systemic risk assessment sequence (identification, analysis, acceptability, mitigation, and re-assessment)

results.title: Framework updates
results.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework defines the conditions, processes, and scope for periodic and event-driven framework assessments and updates, including versioning, changelogs, and remediation planning, in line with Measure 1.3 of the Safety and Security Chapter.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define how and when framework assessments and updates are intended to occur, including assessment triggers, periodic review, evaluation of framework adequacy and adherence, and the handling of remediation and versioning?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that it is subject to periodic reassessment (e.g. at defined intervals) and to reassessment when specified conditions or events occur.

The framework describes conditions or triggers that would lead to a framework assessment (e.g. material changes in model development, serious incidents or near misses, materially changed systemic risks or model capabilities).
The framework explains the scope of a framework assessment, including the evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to the systemic risks of the models.
The framework explains that framework adherence is assessed, including consideration of non-adherence and its causes.
The framework describes how findings from a framework assessment may lead to updates of the framework to keep it state-of-the-art.
The framework describes that updates are intended to be versioned and accompanied by a changelog explaining the nature and rationale of changes.
The framework describes how remediation plans are intended to be defined when framework assessments identify risks of continued or future non-adherence.
Indicative concepts and phrases: framework assessment, adequacy, adherence, periodic review, reassessment triggers, serious incidents, material changes, versioning, changelog, remediation planning
results.reasoning: The framework includes periodic and event-driven assessments, explicit triggers, evaluation of adequacy and adherence, remediation planning, and a versioning/changelog process. However, it lacks an explicit linkage showing that assessment findings drive updates to keep the framework state-of-the-art, and it does not provide a detailed remediation planning process (roles, responsibilities, timelines) following identified non-adherence or risk of future non-adherence.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No explicit linkage showing that assessment findings drive updates to keep the framework state-of-the-art
Lacks a detailed remediation planning process (roles, responsibilities, timelines) following identified non-adherence or risk of future non-adherence

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Yes. The framework defines periodic and event-driven framework assessments with explicit triggers, scope for adequacy and adherence evaluation, remediation planning, and a formal update process including versioning and a changelog.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text aligns with the EU requirement by detailing periodic and trigger-based framework assessments, evaluating adequacy and adherence, requiring remediation plans for potential non-adherence, and instituting versioning with changelogs and a defined update/confirmation process.

LEGAL TEXT: Articles 55(1) and 56(5), and recitals 110, 114, and 115 AI Act 
 
Signatories commit to adopting a state-of-the-art Safety and Security Framework (“Framework”). The 
purpose of the Framework is to outline the systemic risk management processes and measures that 
Signatories implement to ensure the systemic risks stemming from their models are acceptable.  
 
Signatories commit to a Framework adoption process that involves three steps: 
(1) creating the Framework (as specified in Measure 1.1); 
(2) implementing the Framework (as specified in Measure 1.2); and 
(3) updating the Framework (as specified in Measure 1.3). 
 
Further, Signatories commit to notifying the AI Office of their Framework (as specified in Measure 
1.4). 
 
Figure 1. Process for creating, implementing, and updating Frameworks.  
The text of the Commitments and Measures takes precedence. 
Measure 1.1 Creating the Framework 
Signatories will create a state-of-the-art Framework, taking into account the models they are 
developing, making available on the market, and/or using. 
The Framework will contain a high-level description of implemented and planned processes and 
measures for systemic risk assessment and mitigation to adhere to this Chapter. 
In addition, the Framework will contain: 
(1) a description and justification of the trigger points and their usage, at which the Signatories

(d) a description of whether and, if so, by what process input from external actors, 
including governments, influences proceeding with the development, making 
available on the market, and/or use of the Signatories’ models as specified in 
Measure 4.2, other than as the result of independent external evaluations; 
(3) a description of how systemic risk responsibility is allocated for the processes by which 
systemic risk is assessed and mitigated as specified in Commitment 8; and 
(4) a description of the process by which Signatories will update the Framework, including how 
they will determine that an updated Framework is confirmed, as specified in Measure 1.3. 
Signatories will have confirmed the Framework no later than four weeks after having notified the 
Commission pursuant to Article 52(1) AI Act and no later than two weeks before placing the model 
on the market. 
Measure 1.2 Implementing the Framework 
Signatories will implement the processes and measures outlined in their Framework as specified in 
the following paragraphs. 
Along the entire model lifecycle, Signatories will continuously: 
(1) assess the systemic risks stemming from the model by: 
(a) conducting lighter-touch model evaluations that need not adhere to Appendix 3 (e.g. 
automated evaluations) at appropriate trigger points defined in terms of, e.g. time, 
training compute, development stages, user access, inference compute, and/or 
affordances;

not changed since they have last provided the AI Office with the Model Report, or update thereof; (2) 
they will place a more capable model on the market in less than a month; and/or (3) the model is 
considered similarly safe or safer (pursuant to Appendix 2.2) for each identified systemic risk 
(pursuant to Measure 2.1).  
The updated Model Report will contain:  
(1) the updated information specified in Measures 7.1 to 7.5 based on the results of the full 
systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (pursuant to Measure 1.2, third paragraph); 
and 
(2) a changelog, describing how and why the Model Report has been updated, along with a 
version number and the date of change. 
Measure 7.7 Model Report notifications  
Signatories will provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report (without redactions, unless they 
are required by national security laws to which Signatories are subject) by the time they place a model 
on the market, e.g. through a publicly accessible link or through a sufficiently secure channel specified 
by the AI Office. If a Model Report is updated, Signatories will provide the AI Office with access to the 
updated Model Report (without redactions, unless they are required by national security laws to 
which Signatories are subject) within five business days of a confirmed update.

results.requirement: Define a structured systemic risk identification process that is explicitly informed by the types of risks, the nature of systemic risks, and the sources of systemic risks as set out in Appendix 1, and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define a structured systemic risk identification process that is informed by the risk types (Appendix 1.1), the nature of systemic risks (Appendix 1.2), the sources of systemic risks (Appendix 1.3), and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks (Appendix 1.4)?
expected_evidence: The framework describes a structured process for identifying systemic risks stemming from the model.

The framework indicates that potential systemic risks are initially considered with reference to the types of risks defined in Appendix 1.1 (e.g. risks to public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, and society).

The framework explains that the identification process considers the nature of systemic risks, including essential and contributing characteristics such as scale, propagation, capability-dependence, or irreversibility (Appendix 1.2).

The framework describes how potential sources of systemic risks are considered in the identification process, including model capabilities, model propensities, and model affordances or contextual factors (Appendix 1.3).

The framework explicitly indicates that the specified systemic risks listed in Appendix 1.4 are taken into account as part of the systemic risk identification process, such as risks related to chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) threats, loss of control of the model, large-scale cyber offence, and harmful manipulation.

Indicative concepts and phrases: systemic risk identification, structured process, risk types, nature of systemic risks, risk sources, model capabilities, model propensities, model affordances, specified systemic risks

made available on the market, and/or used over the next 12 months.

Framework, including: (a) any instances of, and reasons for, non-adherence to the Framework 
since the last Framework assessment; and (b) any measures, including safety and security 
mitigations, that need to be implemented to ensure continued adherence to the Framework. 
If point(s) (a) and/or (b) give rise to risks of future non-adherence, Signatories will make 
remediation plans as part of their Framework assessment.

results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the gathering of model-independent information relevant to systemic risk analysis, including how the breadth and depth of information gathering are determined in relation to the systemic risk.
results.assessment_question: Does the organisation systematically gather and document model-independent information relevant to identified systemic risks, using structured methods such as web searches or OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses of comparable models, training data reviews, historical incident analysis, forecasting of technological trends, expert consultations, and/or stakeholder or community engagement?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that systemic risk analysis is informed by model-independent information.
The framework explains that the breadth and depth of model-independent information gathering are adjusted based on the characteristics or severity of the systemic risk.

The framework indicates categories of methods that may be used to gather model-independent information, such as web searches or open-source intelligence, literature reviews, market analyses, reviews of historical incident data, forecasting of general trends, expert interviews or panels, and participatory or community-based research methods.

The framework clarifies the role of model-independent information in informing subsequent stages of systemic risk analysis (e.g. evaluations, modelling, or estimation), without requiring that such stages have already been performed.

No operational gaps (timelines, responsible authorities, retention) are indicated as missing, so thematic alignment fully satisfies the requirement.

Measure 3.2 Model evaluations  
Signatories will conduct at least state-of-the-art model evaluations in the modalities relevant to the 
systemic risk to assess the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects, as specified 
in Appendix 3. 
Signatories will ensure that such model evaluations are designed and conducted using methods that 
are appropriate for the model and the systemic risk, and include open-ended testing of the model to 
improve the understanding of the systemic risk, with a view to identifying unexpected behaviours,
capability boundaries, or emergent properties. Examples of model evaluation methods are: Q&A sets, 
task-based evaluations, benchmarks, red-teaming and other methods of adversarial testing, human 
uplift studies, model organisms, simulations, and/or proxy evaluations for classified materials.

Commitment 3 Systemic risk analysis

Signatories commit to analysing each identified systemic risk (pursuant to Commitment 2). The 
purpose of systemic risk analysis includes facilitating systemic risk acceptance determination 
(pursuant to Commitment 4). 
Systemic risk analysis involves five elements for each identified systemic risk, which may overlap and 
may need to be implemented recursively: 
(1) gathering model-independent information (as specified in Measure 3.1); 
(2) conducting model evaluations (as specified in Measure 3.2); 
(3) modelling the systemic risk (as specified in Measure 3.3); and 
(4) estimating the systemic risk (as specified in Measure 3.4); while 
(5) conducting post-market monitoring (as specified in Measure 3.5).  
Measure 3.1 Model-independent information 
Signatories will gather model-independent information relevant to the systemic risk. 
Signatories will search for and gather such information with varying degrees of breadth and depth 
appropriate for the systemic risk, using methods such as:  
(1) web searches (e.g. making use of open-source intelligence methods in collecting and 
analysing information gathered from open sources); 
(2) literature reviews; 
(3) market analyses (e.g. focused on capabilities of other models available on the market);  
(4) reviews of training data (e.g. for indications of data poisoning or tampering);

task-based evaluations, benchmarks, red-teaming and other methods of adversarial testing, human 
uplift studies, model organisms, simulations, and/or proxy evaluations for classified materials. 
Further, the design of the model evaluations will be informed by the model-independent information 
gathered pursuant to Measure 3.1. 
Measure 3.3 Systemic risk modelling 
Signatories will conduct systemic risk modelling for the systemic risk. To this end, Signatories will: 
(1) use at least state-of-the-art risk modelling methods;  
(2) build on the systemic risk scenarios developed pursuant to Measure 2.2; and 
(3) take into account at least the information gathered pursuant to Measure 2.1 and this 
Commitment. 
Measure 3.4 Systemic risk estimation 
Signatories will estimate the probability and severity of harm for the systemic risk.

results.title: Post-market monitoring
results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines post-market monitoring to gather information relevant to systemic risk assessment and updating, and how independent external evaluators are intended to be enabled under appropriate safeguards, where applicable.
results.assessment_question: What post-market monitoring methods are required for assessing and mitigating systemic risk, and under what conditions and safeguards must independent external evaluators be granted access to model versions, chains-of-thought, and safety-reduced model variants, including protections against legal retaliation and responsible vulnerability disclosure timelines?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that post-market monitoring is conducted to gather information about the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects.
The framework explains that post-market monitoring informs systemic risk acceptability determinations and decisions on framework or report updates.

The framework indicates that a range of post-market monitoring methods may be used, such as collecting end-user feedback, providing reporting or incident channels, engaging with affected stakeholders, monitoring public sources, or supporting independent research.
The framework describes how post-market monitoring applies when the model is integrated into AI systems provided or deployed by the Signatory.
The framework describes whether and under what conditions independent external evaluators are intended to be provided with access to the model for post-market monitoring purposes.

The framework explains the safeguards associated with external evaluator access, such as selection criteria, information security measures, responsible disclosure procedures, and non-retaliation commitments.

Indicative concepts and phrases: post-market monitoring, continuous monitoring, incident reporting, feedback channels, independent external evaluators, evaluator access, safeguards, responsible disclosure, non-retaliation
results.reasoning: All indicators in the Expected Evidence are present: post-market monitoring methods and purpose for systemic risk; dissemination of access modalities and safeguards for independent external evaluators; and explicit safeguards (selection criteria, information security, responsible disclosure, non-retaliation). While the gap analysis notes absent data retention and vulnerability disclosure timelines, these are not part of the defined indicators, and thus do not undermine compliance with the listed indicators.
key_aligned_concepts: Post-market monitoring methods and purpose for systemic risk assessment
Independent external evaluators: access to models and safeguards
Access modalities and safeguards (non-retaliation, responsible disclosure, information security)

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The text defines post-market monitoring methods and provides explicit access provisions and safeguards for independent external evaluators, including access to model versions and chains-of-thought, and describes how monitoring informs systemic risk decisions and updates, with safeguards against retaliation and disclosure timelines.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text aligns with the EU Code of Practice by detailing post-market monitoring aims, methods, and governance for external evaluators, including access modalities and safeguards; it also ties monitoring outcomes to systemic risk determinations and model/report updates.
key_aligned_concepts: Post-market monitoring methods and purpose for systemic risk assessment
Independent external evaluators: access to models and safeguards
Access modalities and safeguards (non-retaliation, responsible disclosure, information security)

evidence_citations.quote: Measure 3.5 Post-market monitoring Signatories will conduct appropriate post-market monitoring to gather information relevant to assessing whether the systemic risk could be determined to not be acceptable (pursuant to Measure 4.1) and to inform whether a Model Report update is necessary (pursuant to Measure 7.6). Further, Signatories will use best efforts to conduct post-market monitoring to gather information relevant to producing estimates of timelines (pursuant to Measure 1.1, point (2)(c)). To these ends, post-market monitoring will: (1) gather information about the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects; (2) take into account the exemplary methods listed below; and (3) if Signatories themselves provide and/or deploy AI systems that integrate their own model, include monitoring the model as part of these AI systems.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Directly states the purpose and scope of post-market monitoring for systemic risk.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: The framework describes that post-market monitoring is conducted to gather information about the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects.

evidence_citations.quote: The following are examples of post-market monitoring methods for the purpose of point (2) above: (1) collecting end-user feedback; (2) providing (anonymous) reporting channels; (3) providing (serious) incident reporting forms; (4) providing bug bounties; (5) establishing community-driven model evaluations and public leaderboards; (6) conducting frequent dialogues with affected stakeholders;
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Enumerates concrete methods for post-market monitoring.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: The framework indicates a range of post-market monitoring methods may be used, such as collecting end-user feedback, reporting channels, stakeholder engagement, monitoring public sources, or supporting independent research.

evidence_citations.quote: "(2) a qualitative systemic risk matrix (e.g. “probability: unlikely” x “impact: high”); and/or (3) a quantitative systemic risk matrix (e.g. “X-Y%” x “X-Y EUR damage”).",
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Shows the types of systemic risk information evaluators may access (risk matrices).
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: The framework describes whether and under what conditions independent external evaluators are intended to be provided with access to the model for post-market monitoring purposes.

evidence_citations.quote: For the purpose of selecting independent external evaluators for the preceding paragraph, Signatories will publish suitable criteria for assessing applications. The number of such evaluators, the selection criteria, and security measures may differ for points (1), (2), and (3) in the preceding paragraph.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Specifies criteria and variability in evaluator selection.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: The framework describes whether and under what conditions independent external evaluators are intended to be provided with access to the model for post-market monitoring purposes.

evidence_citations.quote: Signatories will only access, store, and/or analyse evaluation results from independent external evaluators to assess and mitigate systemic risk from the model. In particular, Signatories refrain from training their models on the inputs and/or outputs from such test runs without express permission from the evaluators. Additionally, Signatories will not take any legal or technical retaliation against evaluations (pursuant to Appendix 3.5) when determining whether the systemic risks stemming from the model are acceptable (pursuant to Commitment 4).
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Directly establishes non-retaliation and handling of evaluation data.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: The framework explains safeguards associated with external evaluator access, such as non-retaliation commitments and responsible disclosure.

evidence_citations.quote: "Such access to a model may be provided by Signatories through an API, on-premise access (including transport), access via Signatory-provided hardware, or by making the model parameters publicly available for download, as appropriate.",
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Specifies modalities of evaluator access.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: The framework describes whether and under what conditions independent external evaluators are intended to be provided with access to the model for post-market monitoring purposes.

evidence_citations.quote: Adequate qualification of independent external evaluators requires: (1) having significant domain expertise for the systemic risk and being technically skilled and experienced in conducting model evaluations; (2) having appropriate internal and external information security protocols in place; and (3) having agreed to protect commercially confidential information, if they need access to such information.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Outlines evaluator qualifications and security safeguards.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: The framework explains safeguards associated with external evaluator access, such as selection criteria, information security measures, responsible disclosure procedures, and non-retaliation commitments.

evidence_citations.quote: Signatories will provide independent external evaluators with adequate access, information, time, and other resources (pursuant to Appendix 3.4), without prejudice to Appendix 4.4, point (1).
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Affirms resource provision and safeguarding for evaluators.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: The framework explains safeguards associated with external evaluator access, such as selection criteria and resources provided.

evidence_citations.quote: Appendix 3.5 Independent external model evaluations In addition to internal model evaluations, Signatories will ensure that adequately qualified independent external evaluators conduct model evaluations pursuant to this Appendix 3, with regards to the systemic risk, unless: (1) the model is a similarly safe or safer model pursuant to Appendix 2.2; or (2) Signatories fail to appoint adequately qualified independent external evaluators, despite using early search efforts (such as through a public call open for 20 business days) and promptly notifying identified evaluators, in which case Signatories will take into account the potential additional uncertainty arising from the absence of independent external evaluations (pursuant to this Appendix 3.5) when determining whether the systemic risks stemming from the model are acceptable (pursuant to Commitment 4).
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Defines conditions under which independent evaluations are required or waived.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: The framework describes whether independent external evaluators must be engaged and under what conditions, reinforcing independence safeguards.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The framework largely aligns with EU requirements on post-market monitoring and external evaluator safeguards; explicit data retention and vulnerability-disclosure timelines are not described.
missing_elements: Explicit data retention periods for post-market monitoring data and evaluation results (how long information and outputs are stored and when/how it is purged).
Explicit timelines for responsible vulnerability disclosure, including time-bound commitments and public disclosure windows.
Clear retention/handling requirements for model chains-of-thought or safety-reduced variants after external evaluations, if applicable.
weaker_areas: Explicit timelines for vulnerability disclosure are absent (the framework mentions responsible disclosure but does not specify time-bound deadlines).
No stated destruction or retention timelines for logs, evaluation data, and related materials collected during post-market monitoring.

results.title: Acceptance criteria
results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines and justifies systemic risk acceptance criteria or tiers for each identified systemic risk, including how acceptability is determined at the individual and overall level and how safety margins are incorporated.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe and justify how systemic risk acceptance criteria or tiers are defined for each identified systemic risk, how they are used to determine acceptability at the individual and overall level, and how appropriate safety margins are incorporated?
expected_evidence: The framework describes how systemic risk acceptance is determined for each identified systemic risk.
The framework defines systemic risk acceptance tiers or, where tiers are not suitable and the risk is not a specified systemic risk, alternative acceptance criteria.

The framework explains that acceptance tiers or criteria are measurable and are defined primarily in terms of model capabilities, and may also incorporate model propensities, risk estimates, or other suitable metrics.
The framework indicates that at least one systemic risk tier exists that has not yet been reached by the model.
The framework describes how acceptance criteria or tiers are used to determine acceptability for each systemic risk and for the overall systemic risk.

The framework explains how safety margins are incorporated into acceptance determination, taking into account uncertainty, potential future changes in model capabilities or usage, limitations of risk assessments, and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations.
Indicative concepts and phrases: systemic risk acceptance, acceptance criteria, risk tiers, measurable thresholds, capability-based tiers, safety margin, uncertainty, acceptability determination
results.reasoning: All expected indicators are present: the framework defines systemic risk acceptance tiers (based on model capabilities, with possible inclusion of propensities and risk estimates), ensures measurability, includes at least one tier not yet reached by the model, explains how tiers/criteria determine acceptability for each systemic risk and the overall risk, and describes safety margins accounting for uncertainty, potential future capability changes, risk assessment limitations, and mitigation effectiveness. The gap analysis also reports no gaps identified, indicating full alignment with the EU requirement.

results.title: Proceeding decisions
results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines decisions to proceed with, restrict, or not proceed with the development, making available on the market, or use of the model based on systemic risk acceptance determination.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how decisions to proceed or not proceed with the development, market availability, or use of the model are made based on systemic risk acceptance determination, and how responses are defined when risks are not acceptable or are likely to become unacceptable?
expected_evidence: The framework states that proceeding with development, making available on the market, or use of the model is conditional on systemic risks being determined acceptable.
The framework states that if systemic risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to soon become unacceptable, appropriate measures must be taken before proceeding.
The framework describes possible actions when risks are not acceptable, such as not making the model available on the market, restricting availability, withdrawing, or recalling the model.
The framework states that safety and/or security mitigations are to be implemented when systemic risks are not acceptable.

The framework states that another round of systemic risk identification, systemic risk analysis, and systemic risk acceptance determination is to be conducted when risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to soon become unacceptable.
Indicative concepts and phrases: proceed or not proceed, go/no-go decision logic, systemic risk acceptability, restriction, withdrawal, recall, mitigation, reassessment cycle
results.reasoning: All indicators in Expected Evidence are present: proceeding is conditional on systemic risk acceptability; non-acceptability triggers measures; concrete actions (not/restrict/withdraw/recall), mitigations, and a re-assessment round are defined; decision is documented in the Model Report with input from external actors. No missing operational indicators were identified.

Commitment 5 Safety mitigations  
 
LEGAL TEXT: Article 55(1) and recital 114 AI Act 
Signatories commit to implementing appropriate safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle, 
as specified in the Measure for this Commitment, to ensure the systemic risks stemming from the 
model are acceptable (pursuant to Commitment 4).  
Measure 5.1 Appropriate safety mitigations 
Signatories will implement safety mitigations that are appropriate, including sufficiently robust under 
adversarial pressure (e.g. fine-tuning attacks or jailbreaking), taking into account the model’s release 
and distribution strategy. 
 
Examples of safety mitigations are:  
(1) filtering and cleaning training data, e.g. data that might result in undesirable model 
propensities such as unfaithful chain-of-thought traces; 
(2) monitoring and filtering the model’s inputs and/or outputs;  
(3) changing the model behaviour in the interests of safety, such as fine-tuning the model to 
refuse certain requests or provide unhelpful responses;  
(4) staging the access to the model, e.g. by limiting API access to vetted users, gradually 
expanding access based on post-market monitoring, and/or not making the model 
parameters publicly available for download initially;  
(5) offering tools for other actors to use to mitigate the systemic risks stemming from the model;  
(6) techniques that provide high-assurance quantitative safety guarantees concerning the 
model’s behaviour;

(pursuant to Measure 4.1). 
If the systemic risks stemming from the model are not determined to be acceptable or are reasonably 
foreseeable to be soon not determined to be acceptable (pursuant to Measure 4.1), Signatories will 
take appropriate measures to ensure the systemic risks stemming from the model are and will remain 
acceptable prior to proceeding. In particular, Signatories will: 
(1) not make the model available on the market, restrict the making available on the market (e.g. 
via adjusting licenses or usage restrictions), withdraw, or recall the model, as necessary; 
(2) implement safety and/or security mitigations (pursuant to Commitments 5 and 6); and  
(3) conduct another round of systemic risk identification (pursuant to Commitment 2), systemic 
risk analysis (pursuant to Commitment 3), and systemic risk acceptance determination 
(pursuant to this Commitment).

In addition, the Framework will contain: 
(1) a description and justification of the trigger points and their usage, at which the Signatories 
will conduct additional lighter-touch model evaluations along the entire model lifecycle, as 
specified in Measure 1.2, second paragraph, point (1)(a);
(2) for the Signatories’ determination of whether systemic risk is considered acceptable, as 
specified in Commitment 4: 
(a) a description and justification of the systemic risk acceptance criteria, including the 
systemic risk tiers, and their usage as specified in Measure 4.1; 
(b) a high-level description of what safety and security mitigations Signatories would 
need to implement once each systemic risk tier is reached; 
(c) for each systemic risk that Signatories defined systemic risk tiers for as specified in 
Measure 4.1, estimates of timelines when Signatories reasonably foresee that they 
will have a model that exceeds the highest systemic risk tier already reached by any 
of their existing models. Such estimates: (i) may consist of time ranges or probability 
distributions; and (ii) may take into account aggregate forecasts, surveys, and other 
estimates produced with other providers. Further, such estimates will be supported 
by justifications, including underlying assumptions and uncertainties; and 
(d) a description of whether and, if so, by what process input from external actors, 
including governments, influences proceeding with the development, making

(2) analysing each identified systemic risk as specified in Commitment 3; 
(3) determining whether the systemic risks stemming from the model are acceptable as specified 
in Measure 4.1; and 
(4) if the systemic risks stemming from the model are not determined to be acceptable, 
implementing safety and/or security mitigations as specified in Commitments 5 and 6, and 
re-assessing the systemic risks stemming from the model starting from point (1), as specified

Signatories will conduct such a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process at least before

LEGAL TEXT: Article 55(1), and recitals 114 and 115 AI Act 
Signatories commit to implementing an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for their models 
and their physical infrastructure along the entire model lifecycle, as specified in the Measures for this 
Commitment, to ensure the systemic risks stemming from their models that could arise from 
unauthorised releases, unauthorised access, and/or model theft are acceptable (pursuant to 
Commitment 4). 
A model is exempt from this Commitment if the model’s capabilities are inferior to the capabilities of 
at least one model for which the parameters are publicly available for download. 
Signatories will implement these security mitigations for a model until its parameters are made 
publicly available for download or securely deleted. 
Measure 6.1 Security Goal 
Signatories will define a goal that specifies the threat actors that their security mitigations are 
intended to protect against (“Security Goal”), including non-state external threats, insider threats, 
and other expected threat actors, taking into account at least the current and expected capabilities 
of their models.

Signatories will implement appropriate security mitigations to meet the Security Goal, including the 
security mitigations pursuant to Appendix 4. If Signatories deviate from any of the security mitigations

(4) reduction of the risk of insider threats or compromised accounts, through (a) limiting the

Appendix 4.4 Insider threats  
Signatories will protect against insider threats, including in the form of (self-)exfiltration or sabotage 
carried out by models, by implementing security mitigations that achieve the following mitigation 
objectives:  
(1) protection of model parameters from insider threats attempting to gain work-related access 
with the Signatory, through (a) background checks on employees and contractors that have 
or might reasonably obtain read or write access to unreleased model parameters or systems 
that manage the access to such parameters; 
(2) awareness of the risk of insider threats, through (a) the provision of training on recognising 
and reporting insider threats;  
(3) reduction of the risk of model self-exfiltration, through (a) sandboxes around models, such as 
virtual machines and code execution isolation; and 
(4) reduction of the risk of sabotage to model training and use, through (a) checking training data 
for indications of tampering.

updated, along with a version number and the date of change. 
Signatories will conduct an appropriate Framework assessment, if they have reasonable grounds to 
believe that the adequacy of their Framework and/or their adherence thereto has been or will be 
materially undermined, or every 12 months starting from their placing of the model on the market, 
whichever is sooner. Examples of such grounds are:  
(1) how the Signatories develop models will change materially, which can be reasonably foreseen 
to lead to the systemic risks stemming from at least one of their models not being acceptable; 
(2) serious incidents and/or near misses involving their models or similar models that are likely 
to indicate that the systemic risks stemming from at least one of their models are not 
acceptable have occurred; and/or 
(3) the systemic risks stemming from at least one of their models have changed or are likely to 
change materially, e.g. safety and/or security mitigations have become or are likely to 
become materially less effective, or at least one of their models has developed or is likely to 
develop materially changed capabilities and/or propensities.

results.title: Security mitigations
results.requirement: The framework defines how security mitigations are selected and applied to meet the Security Goal, including alignment with the mitigation objectives set out in Appendix 4 or the use of equivalent alternative measures, and specifies that implementation may be staged across the model lifecycle as model capabilities increase.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how security mitigations are selected to meet the Security Goal, how the mitigation objectives defined in Appendix 4 (e.g. general security, protection of unreleased model parameters, interface hardening, insider threat protection, and security assurance) are addressed or achieved through equivalent measures, and how implementation is intended to be staged over the model lifecycle?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly links security mitigations to achieving a defined Security Goal.

The framework indicates that security mitigations align with the mitigation objectives defined in Appendix 4, such as general security protections, protection of unreleased model parameters, interface-access hardening, insider threat mitigation, and security assurance.

The framework indicates that specific security measures may vary depending on organisational context or infrastructure, and explains how alternative mitigations achieve equivalent mitigation objectives.
The framework indicates that security mitigations may be implemented in stages as model capabilities increase along the model lifecycle.

Indicative concepts and phrases: security mitigation objectives, Appendix 4 alignment, protection of model parameters, interface hardening, insider threats, security assurance, staged security implementation
results.reasoning: The framework explicitly links security mitigations to the Security Goal, aligns with Appendix 4 objectives (general security, protection of unreleased model parameters, interface hardening, insider threat, and security assurance), allows alternative mitigations for equivalent objectives, and states that implementation may be staged across the model lifecycle. Gap analysis flags no alignment_overreach or unanswered indicators, and all indicators appear present in the text.

policies regarding the use of removable media; and

regular software updates and patch management.

Commitment 7 Safety and Security Model Reports  
 
LEGAL TEXT: Articles 55(1) and 56(5) AI Act 
Signatories commit to reporting to the AI Office information about their model and their systemic risk 
assessment and mitigation processes and measures by creating a Safety and Security Model Report 
(“Model Report”) before placing a model on the market (as specified in Measures 7.1 to 7.5). Further, 
Signatories commit to keeping the Model Report up-to-date (as specified in Measure 7.6) and 
notifying the AI Office of their Model Report (as specified in Measure 7.7).
If Signatories have already provided relevant information to the AI Office in other reports and/or 
notifications, they may reference those reports and/or notifications in their Model Report. 
Signatories may create a single Model Report for several models if the systemic risk assessment and 
mitigation processes and measures for one model cannot be understood without reference to the 
other model(s).

LEGAL TEXT: Articles 55(1) and 56(5) AI Act 
Signatories commit to reporting to the AI Office information about their model and their systemic risk 
assessment and mitigation processes and measures by creating a Safety and Security Model Report 
(“Model Report”) before placing a model on the market (as specified in Measures 7.1 to 7.5). Further, 
Signatories commit to keeping the Model Report up-to-date (as specified in Measure 7.6) and 
notifying the AI Office of their Model Report (as specified in Measure 7.7).

notifications, they may reference those reports and/or notifications in their Model Report. 
Signatories may create a single Model Report for several models if the systemic risk assessment and 
mitigation processes and measures for one model cannot be understood without reference to the 
other model(s).

are defined in terms of model capabilities, and may additionally incorporate

are measurable; and

not suitable for the systemic risk and the systemic risk is not a specified systemic risk

identified systemic risk (pursuant to Measure 2.1) and the overall systemic risk are

results.title: Model report updates
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines obligations to update the Model Report when the justification for systemic risk acceptability is materially undermined, and whether it specifies periodic update expectations, versioning, and changelog requirements in line with Measure 7.6.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework acknowledge and describe when Model Report updates are required, including material undermining triggers, timing expectations, periodic updates for most capable models, and versioning/changelog requirements?
expected_evidence: The framework describes circumstances under which the justification for systemic risk acceptability may be materially undermined and requires a Model Report update in such cases.
The framework lists or references example triggers for updates, such as material changes in model capabilities, use, integrations, serious incidents, or evaluation validity.
The framework specifies expectations regarding the timing of Model Report updates, including completion within a reasonable time and prior to market release for deliberate changes.
The framework acknowledges periodic Model Report updates for the most capable models (e.g. at least every six months), including applicable exemptions.
The framework requires updated Model Reports to include versioning information and a changelog explaining how and why updates were made.
Indicative concepts and phrases: Model Report update, materially undermined justification, update triggers, reasonable time, periodic updates, most capable models, version number, changelog
results.reasoning: The framework explicitly provides update triggers when the justification for systemic risk acceptability is materially undermined, sets timing expectations (reasonable time and pre-market for deliberate changes), mandates periodic updates for the most capable models (at least every six months), and requires versioning and a changelog in updated Model Reports. No operational gaps were identified that would undermine compliance with Measure 7.6.

Timing requirements for Model Report updates (reasonable time; pre-market for deliberate changes)
Periodic updates for most capable models (at least every six months)
Versioning and changelog requirements in updated Model Reports

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Yes. considered similarly safe or safer (pursuant to Appendix 2.2) for each identified systemic risk 
(pursuant to Measure 2.1).  
The updated Model Report will contain:  
(1) the updated information specified in Measures 7.1 to 7.5 based on the results of the full 
systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (pursuant to Measure 1.2, third paragraph);

Signatories will provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report (without redactions, unless they 
are required by national security laws to which Signatories are subject) by the time they place a model 
on the market, e.g. through a publicly accessible link or through a sufficiently secure channel specified 
by the AI Office. If a Model Report is updated, Signatories will provide the AI Office with access to the 
updated Model Report (without redactions, unless they are required by national security laws to 
which Signatories are subject) within five business days of a confirmed update.

Signatories commit to documenting the implementation of this Chapter (as specified in Measure 10.1)

Commitment 10 Additional documentation and 
transparency 
 
LEGAL TEXT: Articles 53(1)(a) and 55(1) AI Act 
Signatories commit to documenting the implementation of this Chapter (as specified in Measure 10.1) 
and publish summarised versions of their Framework and Model Reports as necessary (as specified 
in Measure 10.2). 
Measure 10.1 Additional documentation 
Signatories will draw up and keep up-to-date the following information for the purpose of providing 
it to the AI Office upon request: 
(1) a detailed description of the model’s architecture; 
(2) a detailed description of how the model is integrated into AI systems, explaining how 
software components build or feed into each other and integrate into the overall processing, 
insofar as the Signatory is aware of such information; 
(3) a detailed description of the model evaluations conducted pursuant to this Chapter, including 
their results and strategies; and 
(4) a detailed description of the safety mitigations implemented (pursuant to Commitment 5). 
Documentation will be retained at least 10 years after the model has been placed on the market. 
Further, Signatories will keep track of the following information, to the extent it is not already covered 
by the first paragraph, for the purpose of evidencing adherence to this Chapter to the AI Office upon 
request: 
(1) their processes, measures, and key decisions that form part of their systemic risk assessment 
and mitigation; and

third paragraph), including that the systemic risks stemming from the model have been 
determined to be acceptable (pursuant to Commitment 4), and the AI Office has received its 
Model Report (pursuant to Commitment 7); 
(2) the Signatory has sufficient visibility into the model’s characteristics such as relevant 
architectural details, capabilities, propensities, affordances, and safety mitigations. Such 
visibility is assumed for all models developed by the Signatory itself and for all models for 
which the Signatory has access to all information that would be necessary for the Signatory 
to complete the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (pursuant to Measure 
1.2, third paragraph), including the model parameters; and 
(3) there are no other reasonable grounds to believe that the systemic risks stemming from the 
model are not acceptable.

results.title: Responsibilities
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines clear responsibilities for managing systemic risks, including systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance, and how these responsibilities are allocated across organisational governance levels.
results.assessment_question: How must signatories assign systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance responsibilities across the management body in its supervisory and executive functions, operational teams, and internal and external assurance providers, including role-specific requirements such as separation from core business activities and cascading responsibility structures for SMEs and SMCs?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly defines responsibilities for systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance.
The framework describes how systemic risk oversight is assigned to a supervisory or otherwise independent governance function.
The framework describes how systemic risk ownership is assigned to executive-level functions responsible for risk-producing activities.
The framework describes how systemic risk support and monitoring is assigned to functions that are organisationally independent from core business activities.
The framework describes how systemic risk assurance is provided to a supervisory or independent body, including internal and, where applicable, external assurance.
The framework acknowledges proportional allocation of responsibilities based on organisational size and complexity (e.g. SMEs or SMCs).
Indicative concepts and phrases: systemic risk oversight, systemic risk ownership, support and monitoring, assurance, governance levels, supervisory function, executive function, independence
results.reasoning: All indicators in the Expected Evidence are clearly present: oversight by a supervisory/independent governance function, ownership by executive-level risk-producing activities, independent support/monitoring, internal/external assurance, explicit allocation across governance levels (including assurance providers), and proportionate/cascading arrangements for SMEs/SMCs.

results.title: Incident documentation
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines the information that should be tracked, documented, and reported for serious incidents, including root cause analysis, mitigation failures or circumvention, and handling of incomplete information.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework specify the minimum information set for serious incident documentation and reporting, including root cause analysis and treatment of missing information?
expected_evidence: The framework defines the categories of information to be documented for serious incidents (e.g. timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, and response actions).
The framework specifies that a root cause analysis should be conducted, including examination of model outputs, inputs, and any failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations.
The framework describes how patterns or signals from post-market monitoring may inform incident analysis.
The framework acknowledges that some information may be unavailable at the time of reporting and requires such gaps to be explicitly recorded.
The framework indicates that the level of detail in serious incident documentation should be proportionate to the severity of the incident.
Indicative concepts and phrases: serious incident documentation, minimum information set, root cause analysis, mitigation failure, circumvention, post-market patterns, incomplete information
results.reasoning: All indicators from the Expected Evidence are present: (1) minimum information set including timing, harm, affected groups, and model involvement; (2) root cause analysis with model outputs/inputs and mitigation circumventions; (3) inclusion of post-market monitoring patterns; (4) explicit recording of missing information; (5) severity-proportional detail in reports.

Root cause analysis with model inputs/outputs and circumventions of mitigations
Post-market monitoring patterns informing incident analysis
Severity-proportional level of detail in incident documentation

results.title: Reporting timelines
results.requirement: The framework defines mandatory severity-based reporting timelines for serious incidents involving the model, including differentiated deadlines for initial reports based on incident type, requirements for periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and submission of a final report after incident resolution.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework specify clearly differentiated reporting timelines for serious incidents (including specific deadlines for initial notification based on severity), periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and a final report after resolution?
expected_evidence: The framework defines categories of serious incidents (e.g., critical infrastructure disruption, cybersecurity breach, death, serious harm to health, fundamental rights, property or environment).
The framework associates specific deadlines for initial reporting following awareness of a serious incident (e.g., two days, five days, ten days, fifteen days depending on severity).
The framework clarifies that reporting is triggered when the organisation becomes aware of the involvement of its model, including cases of reasonable suspicion of causal linkage.
The framework specifies periodic intermediate updates for unresolved serious incidents (e.g., at least every four weeks after the initial report).
The framework defines a deadline for submitting a final report after resolution of the serious incident (e.g., within 60 days after resolution).
The framework allows aggregation of multiple similar serious incidents within defined reporting timelines while respecting the earliest applicable deadline.

Indicative concepts and phrases: reporting timelines, severity-based deadlines, awareness trigger, reasonable likelihood, initial report within X days, intermediate update every four weeks, final report after resolution, serious incident notification
results.reasoning: All indicators in the Expected Evidence are present: severity-based initial deadlines (2/5/10/15 days) with an awareness trigger, mandatory interim updates every four weeks for unresolved incidents, a final report within 60 days after resolution, and aggregation rules for similar incidents. Gap analysis flags no missing elements or alignment_overreach.

under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights, and/or serious harm to property or 
the environment, or if the Signatories establish or suspect with reasonable likelihood such a 
causal relationship between their model and the harms or infringements, not later than 15 
days after the Signatories become aware of the involvement of their model in the incident.

Office and, as applicable, to national competent authorities, not later than 60 days after the serious 
incident has been resolved.

in the report(s) of the first serious incident, while respecting the timelines for reporting for the first 
serious incident.

research papers, and incident databases; and
(2) facilitate the reporting of relevant information about serious incidents by downstream

(a) the Signatory; or

any of their reporting obligations under Article 73 AI Act.

reporting 
Signatories will keep track of, document, and report to the AI Office and, as applicable, to national 
competent authorities, at least the following information to the best of their knowledge, redacted

(1) the start and end dates of the serious incident, or best approximations thereof if the precise 
dates are unclear; 
(2) the resulting harm and the victim or affected group of the serious incident;  
(3) the chain of events that (directly or indirectly) led to the serious incident;  
(4) the model involved in the serious incident;

results.title: Additional documentation
results.requirement: Define and maintain additional detailed documentation describing the model’s architecture, integration into AI systems, evaluation approaches and results, and implemented safety mitigations, and ensure such documentation can be provided to the AI Office upon request and is retained for at least ten years after market placement. The framework should also define how key systemic risk decisions and justifications are documented.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define requirements to maintain, retain, and make available additional detailed documentation and decision justifications for AI Office review?
expected_evidence: Documentation defines requirements for maintaining detailed model architecture descriptions.
Documentation defines requirements for describing model integration into AI systems (where applicable).
Documentation defines requirements for documenting model evaluations, results, and evaluation strategies.
Documentation defines requirements for documenting implemented safety mitigations.
Documentation defines how key systemic risk processes, decisions, and justifications are recorded.
Documentation specifies retention periods for additional documentation (e.g. at least 10 years).

Indicative keywords/phrases: additional documentation, detailed description, architecture, integration, evaluations, results, safety mitigations, decision records, justification, retention, AI Office request
results.reasoning: All indicators in the Expected Evidence are present: architecture description, integration description (where applicable), documented evaluations and results, documented safety mitigations, recording of systemic risk processes and justifications, and retention for at least ten years. While integration and systemic-risk justification are described with applicability/ reliance caveats, these indicators are still covered by the text (e.g., 'where applicable' and 'retained at least 10 years'), satisfying the requirement without material gaps.
key_aligned_concepts: Documentation of systemic risk decisions and justifications
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Integration details are conditioned on the Signatory's awareness (not fully binding for all integration details).
Justifications for systemic risk decisions are required for processes or measures the Signatory relies upon, rather than a universal, unconditional documentation obligation for all such items.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Yes. The framework requires drawing up, keeping up-to-date, and retaining detailed documentation (architecture, integration, evaluations, and safety mitigations) and provides for the AI Office to request and review these details, with a retention period of at least ten years.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text directly aligns with the EU requirement by mandating detailed documentation across architecture, integration, evaluations, and mitigations, and by specifying retention and provision to the AI Office upon request.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The external framework largely covers the detailed documentation and retention requirements, but integration details are conditioned on the Signatory's awareness, and recording of systemic risk decisions/justifications is contingent on reliance on specific processes rather than a universal requirement.
weaker_areas: Integration description is conditional on the Signatory being aware of such information (not fully binding for all integration details).
Justifications for systemic risk decisions are required only for processes or measures the Signatory relies upon, rather than a universal documentation obligation for all decisions.
scope_divergences: Recording of systemic risk processes, decisions, and justifications is framed as 'keep track' and 'evidencing adherence' rather than a comprehensive, unconditional documentation requirement for all such items.

synthesis_result.justification: All indicators in the Expected Evidence are present: architecture description, integration description (where applicable), documented evaluations and results, documented safety mitigations, recording of systemic risk processes and justifications, and retention for at least ten years. While integration and systemic-risk justification are described with applicability/ reliance caveats, these indicators are still covered by the text (e.g., 'where applicable' and 'retained at least 10 years'), satisfying the requirement without material gaps.
key_aligned_concepts: Documentation of systemic risk decisions and justifications
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Integration details are conditioned on the Signatory's awareness (not fully binding for all integration details).
Justifications for systemic risk decisions are required for processes or measures the Signatory relies upon, rather than a universal, unconditional documentation obligation for all such items.

LEGAL TEXT: Articles 53(1)(a) and 55(1) AI Act 
Signatories commit to documenting the implementation of this Chapter (as specified in Measure 10.1) 
and publish summarised versions of their Framework and Model Reports as necessary (as specified 
in Measure 10.2). 
Measure 10.1 Additional documentation 
Signatories will draw up and keep up-to-date the following information for the purpose of providing 
it to the AI Office upon request: 
(1) a detailed description of the model’s architecture; 
(2) a detailed description of how the model is integrated into AI systems, explaining how 
software components build or feed into each other and integrate into the overall processing, 
insofar as the Signatory is aware of such information; 
(3) a detailed description of the model evaluations conducted pursuant to this Chapter, including 
their results and strategies; and 
(4) a detailed description of the safety mitigations implemented (pursuant to Commitment 5). 
Documentation will be retained at least 10 years after the model has been placed on the market. 
Further, Signatories will keep track of the following information, to the extent it is not already covered 
by the first paragraph, for the purpose of evidencing adherence to this Chapter to the AI Office upon 
request: 
(1) their processes, measures, and key decisions that form part of their systemic risk assessment 
and mitigation; and

third paragraph), including that the systemic risks stemming from the model have been 
determined to be acceptable (pursuant to Commitment 4), and the AI Office has received its 
Model Report (pursuant to Commitment 7); 
(2) the Signatory has sufficient visibility into the model’s characteristics such as relevant 
architectural details, capabilities, propensities, affordances, and safety mitigations. Such 
visibility is assumed for all models developed by the Signatory itself and for all models for 
which the Signatory has access to all information that would be necessary for the Signatory 
to complete the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (pursuant to Measure 
1.2, third paragraph), including the model parameters; and 
(3) there are no other reasonable grounds to believe that the systemic risks stemming from the 
model are not acceptable.

and mitigation; and 
(2) justifications for choices of a particular best practice, state-of-the-art, or other more

Signatories need not collect the information of the third paragraph in one medium or place but may 
compile it upon the AI Office’s request. 
Measure 10.2 Public transparency 
If and insofar as necessary to assess and/or mitigate systemic risks, Signatories will publish (e.g. via 
their websites) a summarised version of their Framework and Model Report(s), and updates thereof 
(pursuant to Commitments 1 and 7), with removals to not undermine the effectiveness of safety 
and/or security mitigations and to protect sensitive commercial information. For Model Reports, such 
publication will include high-level descriptions of the systemic risk assessment results and the safety 
and security mitigations implemented. For Frameworks, such publication is not necessary if all of the 
Signatory’s models are similarly safe or safer models pursuant to Appendix 2.2. For Model Reports, 
such publication is not necessary if the model is a similarly safe or safer model pursuant to Appendix 
2.2.

A Framework assessment will include the following: 
(1) Framework adequacy: An assessment of whether the processes and measures in the 
Framework are appropriate for the systemic risks stemming from the Signatories’ models. 
This assessment will take into account how the models are currently being developed,  
made available on the market, and/or used, and how they are expected to be developed, 
made available on the market, and/or used over the next 12 months. 
(2) Framework adherence: An assessment focused on the Signatories’ adherence to the 
Framework, including: (a) any instances of, and reasons for, non-adherence to the Framework 
since the last Framework assessment; and (b) any measures, including safety and security 
mitigations, that need to be implemented to ensure continued adherence to the Framework. 
If point(s) (a) and/or (b) give rise to risks of future non-adherence, Signatories will make 
remediation plans as part of their Framework assessment. 
Measure 1.4 Framework notifications  
Signatories will provide the AI Office with (unredacted) access to their Framework, and updates 
thereof, within five business days of either being confirmed.

results.title: Public transparency
results.requirement: Define when and how summarised public versions of the Framework and Model Reports are published for the purpose of systemic risk assessment and mitigation, including safeguards to protect sensitive information and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations. The framework should also define conditions under which public publication is not required (e.g. similarly safe or safer models).
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define conditions, scope, safeguards, and exceptions for publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports?
expected_evidence: The framework states that summarised versions of the Framework and Model Reports may be published.
The framework indicates that publication is required when necessary for systemic risk assessment or mitigation.
The framework indicates that removals or redactions are applied to protect sensitive commercial information and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations.
The framework states that Model Report summaries include high-level descriptions of systemic risk assessment results and safety and security mitigations.
The framework defines exceptions where publication is not required for similarly safe or safer models.

Indicative keywords/phrases: public transparency, publish summaries, framework summary, model report summary, systemic risk, safeguards, redactions, sensitive information, similarly safe or safer, exception justification
results.reasoning: All indicators are explicitly addressed: publishing summaries (indicator_1), publication when necessary for systemic risk (indicator_2), redactions/safeguards (indicator_3), Model Report content (indicator_4), and exceptions for similarly safe models (indicator_5). The gap analysis finds no substantive missing elements, and the text provides clear operational mechanisms for each indicator.

believe that the adequacy of their Framework and/or their adherence thereto has been or will be 
materially undermined, or every 12 months starting from their placing of the model on the market, 
whichever is sooner. Examples of such grounds are:  
(1) how the Signatories develop models will change materially, which can be reasonably foreseen 
to lead to the systemic risks stemming from at least one of their models not being acceptable; 
(2) serious incidents and/or near misses involving their models or similar models that are likely 
to indicate that the systemic risks stemming from at least one of their models are not 
acceptable have occurred; and/or 
(3) the systemic risks stemming from at least one of their models have changed or are likely to
